name: Carcinogenic Status Is The Bare Label Column
description: molecule.label is '+' for carcinogenic and '-' for non-carcinogenic, and how it is projected depends on what the question asks for. Most often the question points at one molecule, however it is identified — through an atom, an element it contains, a bond, or a ranking — and asks only whether it is carcinogenic, as in 'identify whether the compound containing calcium is carcinogenic' or 'is the molecule with the most double bonds carcinogenic'. That answer is the single bare column molecule.label: no second column, and no rewriting of the code into 'YES' or 'NO'. When the question instead names several molecules and asks for their labels, the identifier is part of the answer, because otherwise the labels cannot be told apart, so project molecule_id together with the bare label. When the question asks two things in sequence, first which molecule something belongs to and then to state whether that molecule is carcinogenic or not, the second part is a spoken yes-or-no rather than a code, so project the molecule_id and IIF(label = '+', 'YES', 'NO'). Counting, percentage and 'how many are non-carcinogenic' questions filter on label = '+' or '-' and project no label at all. Element codes are lowercase, so chlorine is 'cl' and carbon is 'c'.
sql: SELECT T2.label FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN molecule AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.element = 'ca'

name: Connected Atoms Project Both Endpoints
description: When the answer is the atoms that are connected or bonded to something — 'identify all the atoms that are connected to the atoms of the TR181 molecule', 'what are the atoms that can bond with the atom that has the element lead' — project both endpoint columns, connected.atom_id and connected.atom_id2, in that order. A single endpoint column is not the answer, because a connection is a pair. Reach the pair by joining atom to connected on atom.atom_id = connected.atom_id and filter the anchor on atom, so a molecule anchor is atom.molecule_id = 'TR181' and an element anchor is atom.element = 'pb'. This two-column shape applies only when the answer is atom ids. When the answer is an element, project the single atom.element column and nothing else: 'what elements are in the TR004_8_9 bond atoms' returns one element column, joining atom to connected and filtering connected.bond_id = 'TR004_8_9'. Related phrasings: atoms connected to, atoms that can bond with, identify all connected atoms.
sql: SELECT T2.atom_id, T2.atom_id2 FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN connected AS T2 ON T2.atom_id = T1.atom_id WHERE T1.molecule_id = 'TR181'

name: Bond Questions Scoped By Molecule Skip The Connected Table
description: atom and bond both carry molecule_id, and which of the two ways to relate them is right depends on what the question is scoped by. When the scope is a molecule — molecules that have a single, double or triple bond, the elements or atoms inside such a molecule, a count or percentage of such molecules, or a named molecule together with a bond type — join atom directly to bond on molecule_id and put nothing in between. That is a statement about a molecule containing both the element and the bond, not about the atom sitting on that particular bond, so routing through connected narrows it to bond membership and returns far too few rows. Use connected only when the bond itself is the subject: what type of bond an element is in, the atoms or elements that make up one named bond, or the members of all bonds of a type. The pairing may be written either as atom joined straight to bond, or as atom joined to molecule and molecule joined to bond, which is the same relation threaded through the molecule roster; the roster omits some molecule_ids that atom and bond carry, so the second form answers over the named compounds only. The direct join repeats each atom once for every bond in its molecule, and that fan-out is intended. When the answer counts or identifies molecules, or counts how many kinds of element occur, apply DISTINCT to that column so the repeats do not inflate it. When the answer lists atoms or elements, returns an atom id, or measures a composition across atoms, leave the repeated rows in place and count them as they come. bond_type is '-' single, '=' double, '#' triple, and element codes are lowercase.
sql: SELECT DISTINCT T1.molecule_id FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T1.element = 'n' AND T2.bond_type = '='

name: An Average Is Taken Over Molecules
description: An average number is a count taken inside each instance of whatever the question makes the subject of the average, then averaged over those instances, and the wording says which entity that is. When the count sits inside molecules — the average number of atoms of an element in molecules of a given kind, or on average how many bonds of a type such molecules have — group by molecule_id, count the matching rows in each group, and wrap that in an outer AVG, so the number of molecules is the denominator. When the atoms are the subject instead, as in the average number of bonds that the atoms of an element have, the figure is per atom: divide a COUNT of the bond rows by a COUNT of the atoms in one flat query joining atom to connected, with no grouping and no subquery. Read the denominator off the subject rather than defaulting to either shape. Where the subject is the molecule, a single ratio over the joined rows is wrong: AVG(CASE WHEN element = '<code>' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), or a SUM of matching rows divided by a COUNT of atoms, gives the fraction of rows that match rather than a count per molecule, and lands orders of magnitude low. In the per-molecule count the joined rows are counted as they come, without DISTINCT, because when atom is joined to bond on molecule_id each atom repeats once per bond of that molecule and the intended figure counts those repeats, which is why the averages are large. Related phrasings: calculate the average number of, on average how many.
sql: SELECT AVG(bromine_count) FROM (SELECT T1.molecule_id, COUNT(T1.element) AS bromine_count FROM atom AS T1 INNER JOIN bond AS T2 ON T1.molecule_id = T2.molecule_id WHERE T2.bond_type = '=' AND T1.element = 'br' GROUP BY T1.molecule_id) AS bromine_counts
